bibl.title: MEHDIE: The Middle East Heritage Data Integration Endeavor

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: Can historical Middle Eastern datasets be linked by matching place names directly between the domain's own languages, rather than by transliterating them into Latin script or routing them through a general-purpose gazetteer?
span.quote: The multi-modal entity resolution tool we are developing will utilise spatial (geo-coordinates), temporal (dates/periods) and textual information about a pair of place/person records to help identify the semantic relationship between them.

span.label: Argues, from a worked example, that a general authority file under-covers a specialist domain's own vocabulary, and that intra-domain matching beats routing through a central one.
span.quote: The advantages of intra-domain transliteration for matching opens a meta-discussion on approaches for linked open data and the preference of a “bottom-up” intra-domain strategy over a centralised one.

span.label: method
span.quote: We are building a multi-modal entity resolution tool that utilizes the spatial, temporal, and textual information about a pair of place records to help identify the semantic relation between them.

span.label: cross-lingual toponym entity matching
span.quote: The mission to connect data on the Middle eastern history domain is faced with special challenges: the scarcity of vowels in Semitic scripts, the indeterminacy of pronunciation and transliteration of written toponyms, and varying practices of naming and classifying places.

span.label: system-or-tool-building
span.quote: The multi-modal entity resolution tool we are developing will utilise spatial (geo-coordinates), temporal (dates/periods) and textual information about a pair of place/person records to help identify the semantic relationship between them.

span.label: Matching uses three kinds of evidence at once - coordinates, dates and the text of the name - rather than name similarity alone
span.quote: We are building a multi-modal entity resolution tool that utilizes the spatial, temporal, and textual information about a pair of place records to help identify the semantic relation between them.

span.label: Transliterating between two Semitic languages preserves the ambiguity of both instead of forcing a decision, which is why it beats going through Latin script
span.quote: This shows the power of transliteration between semitic languages that reduces, rather than adds ambiguity: Neither Arabic nor Hebrew explicate the sound that is expressed in English by the first i and the e in the name.

span.label: Latin transliteration fails because it demands vowels the source scripts never wrote
span.quote: Therefore, transliteration to latin script could not deduce an acceptable transliteration.

span.label: Every candidate match is returned with a confidence and an account of which method produced it, so a human can judge it
span.quote: Also visible in the figure are the confidence measure and the explanation of the matching methods that yielded the candidate.

span.label: General gazetteers barely cover the Semitic-script toponyms this domain runs on
span.note: what this limits: any reliance on general gazetteers for this domain: GEONAMES AND THE GETTY THESAURUS ... CONTAIN FEW, IF ANY, TOPONYMS IN THE SEMITIC SCRIPTS relevant to the sources
span.quote: Geonames and the Getty Thesaurus of geographic names are two such resources, but they contain few, if any, toponyms in the Semitic scripts relevant to the sources of Middle Eastern History.

span.label: Even Wikidata, which is multilingual by design, matches poorly against these sources
span.note: what this limits: Wikidata reconciliation specifically: EVEN WIKIDATA, WHICH IS ESSENTIALLY MULTILINGUAL, SHOWS LOW RECALL WHEN MATCHING AGAINST THEM
span.quote: Even Wikidata, which is essentially multilingual, shows low recall when matching against them.

span.label: Where general resources do cover the domain it is the major cities, not the smaller settlements or the historic variants
span.note: what this limits: the coverage that general resources do provide: they include forms that DENOTE MAJOR, WELL KNOWN CITIES, BUT VERY LITTLE HISTORIC VARIANTS OF THE LESSER KNOWN SETTLEMENTS
span.quote: Such general gazetteers may include contemporary Arabic, Hebrew or Syriac forms that denote major, well known cities, but very little historic variants of the lesser known settlements.

span.label: The domain's own scripts make the problem harder before any tool is applied: missing vowels, uncertain pronunciation, and no settled naming practice
span.note: what this limits: every matching result in the domain: THE SCARCITY OF VOWELS IN SEMITIC SCRIPTS, THE INDETERMINACY OF PRONUNCIATION AND TRAN[sliteration] make the problem hard before any tool is applied
span.quote: The mission to connect data on the Middle eastern history domain is faced with special challenges: the scarcity of vowels in Semitic scripts, the indeterminacy of pronunciation and transliteration of written toponyms, and varying practices of naming and classifying places.

span.label: Even the successful transliteration is one of several possible forms, not a unique answer
span.note: what this limits: any successful match treated as unique: the Hebrew-to-Arabic transliteration used was ONE OF TWO POSSIBLE TRANSLITERATIONS
span.quote: we could easily find the match thanks to the transliteration of the Hebrew form to the Arabic form بلبيس, one of two possible transliterations

span.label: transliteration - into Latin script: the usual move, which fails here because it requires vowels the source never wrote
span.quote: Therefore, transliteration to latin script could not deduce an acceptable transliteration.

span.label: transliteration - between Semitic languages: preserves the same indeterminacy on both sides, so it narrows candidates instead of multiplying them
span.quote: The similarity between semitic languages, however, means that direct transliteration between semitic languages would be much more efficient in creating candidates for matching that transliteration into Latin script languages.

span.label: the place name - as written in a nineteenth-century edition: בלביש, with an archaic final consonant
span.quote: The Hebrew toponym for the city of Bilbeis on the Nile’s delta (spelled “Bilbays” in Adler’s translation of Benjamin of Tudela) was mentioned in the 19th century edition of Benjamin of Tudela’s itinerary in the Hebrew form בלביש.

span.label: the place name - as written in contemporary Hebrew: בילביס, with an added vowel and a different final letter - and the authority holds only this one
span.quote: Wikidata currently includes a Hebrew alternative variant without the additional vowel, but not a variant with the more archaic letter ‘ ש’ (Wikidata contributors, "Q393495").

span.label: linked data strategy - centralised: reconcile every source to one external authority, which is the default assumption
span.quote: A common way to identify places, their locations and other information about them is to reconcile the source place names with unique identifiers from an external Gazetteer.

span.label: linked data strategy - bottom-up and intra-domain: match the domain's datasets against each other first, which this paper argues for
span.quote: The advantages of intra-domain transliteration for matching opens a meta-discussion on approaches for linked open data and the preference of a “bottom-up” intra-domain strategy over a centralised one.

span.label: phenomenon: cross-lingual toponym entity matching
span.note: a second reading reaching the same value. Recorded: cross-lingual toponym entity matching — a second reading reaching the same value from a different sentence. Not applied - a person decides.
span.quote: MEHDIE , the Middle East Heritage Data Integration Endeavour is a project at Haifa University and Aalborg University, dedicated to facilitating semantic integration of knowledge sources related to the history of the Middle East, using innovative data integration methods.

span.label: extends → World Historical Gazetteer (Grossner and Mostern 2021)
span.quote: In the demonstration we present tools related to spatial data, which we hope to integrate into the World Historical Gazetteer (Grossner and Mostern 2021) system to enhance its capabilities for inter-dataset matching.

span.label: builds-on → Historical Middle East Data Alliance (Hist-ME)
span.quote: The system we are developing at MEHDI facilitates collaboration between Hist-ME ’s partners towards this vision.

span.label: extends → the World Historical Gazetteer, which the matching tools are intended to enhance
span.quote: In the demonstration we present tools related to spatial data, which we hope to integrate into the World Historical Gazetteer (Grossner and Mostern 2021) system to enhance its capabilities for inter-dataset matching.

span.label: supports → the Hist-ME vision of connecting monolingual and intra-religious data silos
span.quote: The Historical Middle East Data Alliance (Hist-ME) was initiated by Nathan P. Gibson at the Linked Pasts 2021 conference with a joint vision of connecting intra-religious and monolingual silos of disconnected data into a linked contextual wealth of knowledge.

span.label: critiques → reconciliation to general-purpose external gazetteers as the default linked-data strategy
span.quote: Such general gazetteers may include contemporary Arabic, Hebrew or Syriac forms that denote major, well known cities, but very little historic variants of the lesser known settlements.

span.label: transliteration —operationalised-as→ entity resolution
span.quote: Using the transliteration tool in our system to match against Arabic datasets such as Usaybia , Damast , ‘Al-Ṯurayya gazetteer (Romanov and Seydi, 2019) and from a dataset of toponyms from Yaqut al-Hamawi’s Mu 'jam ul-Buldān, we could easily find the match thanks to the transliteration of the Hebrew form to the Arabic form بلبيس, one of two possible transliterations.

span.label: Semitic scripts —causes→ toponyms
span.quote: The mission to connect data on the Middle eastern history domain is faced with special challenges: the scarcity of vowels in Semitic scripts, the indeterminacy of pronunciation and transliteration of written toponyms, and varying practices of naming and classifying places.

span.label: Wikidata —is-a→ gazetteer
span.quote: Even Wikidata, which is essentially multilingual, shows low recall when matching against them.

span.label: Geonames —is-a→ gazetteer
span.quote: Geonames and the Getty Thesaurus of geographic names are two such resources, but they contain few, if any, toponyms in the Semitic scripts relevant to the sources of Middle Eastern History.

span.label: Getty Thesaurus of geographic names —is-a→ gazetteer
span.quote: Geonames and the Getty Thesaurus of geographic names are two such resources, but they contain few, if any, toponyms in the Semitic scripts relevant to the sources of Middle Eastern History.

span.label: intra-domain —contrasted-with→ linked open data
span.quote: The advantages of intra-domain transliteration for matching opens a meta-discussion on approaches for linked open data and the preference of a “bottom-up” intra-domain strategy over a centralised one.

span.label: gazetteer —operationalised-as→ entity resolution
span.quote: A common way to identify places, their locations and other information about them is to reconcile the source place names with unique identifiers from an external Gazetteer.

span.label: confidence measure —part-of→ entity resolution
span.quote: Also visible in the figure are the confidence measure and the explanation of the matching methods that yielded the candidate.

span.label: World Historical Gazetteer —is-a→ gazetteer
span.quote: In the demonstration we present tools related to spatial data, which we hope to integrate into the World Historical Gazetteer (Grossner and Mostern 2021) system to enhance its capabilities for inter-dataset matching.

span.label: Benjamin of Tudela —part-of→ toponyms
span.quote: in this case a dataset of the Hebrew toponyms from Benjamin of Tudela’s travelog collected in the framework of the TraveLab project (Rusinek and Shalit 2022), and Damast Multilingual Dataset from the Dhimmis and & Muslims project (Franke and Kock 2023).

span.label: Hist-ME —part-of→ intra-domain
span.quote: The results of our work with the different datasets of Hist-ME member projects may also constitute an argument in favour of intra-domain collaboration.

span.label: prosopographic —contrasted-with→ toponyms
span.quote: Several projects have been dedicated in recent years to the aggregation of geographic and prosopographic data on Middle Eastern History.

span.label: multilinguality —contrasted-with→ Wikidata
span.quote: Even Wikidata, which is essentially multilingual, shows low recall when matching against them.

span.label: General-purpose gazetteers carry almost none of the Semitic-script toponyms that Middle Eastern historical sources actually use.
span.quote: Geonames and the Getty Thesaurus of geographic names are two such resources, but they contain few, if any, toponyms in the Semitic scripts relevant to the sources of Middle Eastern History.

span.label: Wikidata, although multilingual, also matches these sources poorly.
span.quote: Even Wikidata, which is essentially multilingual, shows low recall when matching against them.

span.label: A concrete gap: Wikidata holds a modern Hebrew variant of the toponym but not the archaic spelling the historical source uses.
span.quote: Wikidata currently includes a Hebrew alternative variant without the additional vowel, but not a variant with the more archaic letter

span.label: Matching between two Semitic languages reduces ambiguity, whereas transliterating either into Latin script adds it.
span.quote: This shows the power of transliteration between semitic languages that reduces, rather than adds ambiguity

span.label: The authors draw a general conclusion for linked open data: prefer a bottom-up, intra-domain strategy over a centralised one.
span.quote: opens a meta-discussion on approaches for linked open data and the preference of a “bottom-up” intra-domain strategy over a centralised one

span.label: general gazetteers including Wikidata have low recall against Semitic-script historical toponyms
span.quote: Even Wikidata, which is essentially multilingual, shows low recall when matching against them.

span.label: transliteration between Semitic languages reduces ambiguity where transliteration into Latin script cannot resolve it at all
span.quote: This shows the power of transliteration between semitic languages that reduces, rather than adds ambiguity: Neither Arabic nor Hebrew explicate the sound that is expressed in English by the first i and the e in the name.

span.label: the worked case: the archaic Hebrew spelling matched its Arabic form directly, while the authority held only the modern Hebrew variant
span.quote: Wikidata currently includes a Hebrew alternative variant without the additional vowel, but not a variant with the more archaic letter ‘ ש’ (Wikidata contributors, "Q393495").

span.label: the results are offered as an argument for intra-domain collaboration over centralised reconciliation
span.quote: The results of our work with the different datasets of Hist-ME member projects may also constitute an argument in favour of intra-domain collaboration.

span.label: reconciliation against a gazetteer
span.quote: A common way to identify places, their locations and other information about them is to reconcile the source place names with unique identifiers from an external Gazetteer.
